title: How scientists used AI to create ultra-stable, freezer-free mRNA vaccines
key_facts: MIT engineers used an AI-driven framework called AGENT (Bayesian optimization with a Gaussian process model) to stabilize lipid nanoparticles carrying mRNA, in a Nature Biotechnology study.
They worked on formulations used in the Moderna and Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccines.
In six rounds the platform reached 100 percent formulation stability and found a candidate for animal tests.
Dried formulations kept full bioactivity at 37 degrees Celsius for over two months and at room temperature for a year.
Mice given long-stored particles had immune responses equal to freshly prepared vaccine.
The formulation also worked in microneedle patches in rodents and non-human primates, with immune responses comparable to liquid injections.
Ana Jaklenec, a principal investigator and senior coauthor, spoke to DDN.
quote_evidence: These formulations helped retain 100 percent bioactivity at 37 degrees Celsius for over two months — eliminating the need for ultra-cold storage completely.
Mice vaccinated with these long-stored particles showed immune responses equivalent to those given freshly prepared vaccines.
why_it_matters_hint: Could remove cold-chain needs for mRNA vaccines, but results are in cells and animals only.
notes: Preclinical (cells, mice, non-human primates). The article says the formulation 'eliminates' ultra-cold storage; we keep it as a study result.
